title: T1021.005 — Remote Services: VNC
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services: VNC with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: Scan for VNC
steps.caption: VNC (Virtual Network Computing) shows and controls another computer's screen. The attacker sweeps the internet for open port 5900 and finds an old support server. Tooling like this often stays exposed long after the project that needed it has ended.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Guess the VNC password
steps.caption: The attacker throws a word list at the VNC password. Most VNC servers do NOT log failed attempts, and that is the blind spot: the endpoint stays silent. Only the firewall notices many short connections to one port.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Full desktop control
steps.caption: The attacker now sees the screen and moves the mouse like a real person. A VNC session is full desktop control, not just a command shell. The only trace is one long, steady flow on port 5900.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Disable protection from the tray
steps.caption: The attacker clicks the antivirus icon in the system tray and stops it. Windows records this as Event 7036, and Sysmon logs the net.exe process. These side effects are some of the few endpoint clues VNC attacks leave.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Install a hidden VNC for persistence
steps.caption: The attacker drops a small hidden VNC server into a public folder and starts it at every login through a Run key. This access survives reboots and password changes. Registry and process logs catch it even though VNC itself logs nothing.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Browse files and card data
steps.caption: The attacker browses folders, dumps the payment app's memory, and copies the results out. Screen sharing makes this look like a person moving files. The egress volume is the loud part, and the netflow record sees it.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.caption: The same weak password opens the store server. One shared support password is how a single store becomes a whole chain. The attacker now reaches backups and store data from the same viewer window.
